n: Job replies to Eliphaz’s second speech. Rather than defend himself point by point, he first tells his friends how their words feel to him.
Job has heard all this before. His friends came to comfort him (2:11), but their comfort only adds to his misery.

f.g: Literally “comforters of trouble” — people whose comfort brings more pain.

n: He turns Eliphaz’s charge of “windy words” (15:2) back on him: will your empty speeches ever end? What drives you to keep answering?

f.g: Literally “words of wind,” echoing Eliphaz’s jab in 15:2.

n: If their places were reversed, Job admits, he could easily pile up speeches and shake his head in scorn at them too.

f.g: A gesture of mockery or contempt.

n: But Job says he would use his words to strengthen and soothe them. He describes the kind of friend he wishes they were.

f.g: Assuage = ease or soften. Job models what real comfort looks like.

n: Neither speaking nor staying silent brings Job any relief. His pain stays with him either way.
Job feels exhausted by God, who has stripped away his family and household. He shifts between speaking about God and to God.

f.g: Job’s household and family, now gone (1:13-19).

n: His shriveled, wasted body seems to testify against him — as if his suffering proves he is guilty, just as the friends claim.

f.g: Gauntness from illness; Job’s body has become a “witness” the friends use against him.

n: Job uses fierce animal imagery: he feels as if God has torn him like a beast and glared at him like an enemy.

f.w: gnasheth upon me with his teeth

n: Now a crowd joins in, gaping, slapping his face, and gathering against him. Many readers see in this a foreshadowing of the Savior’s mistreatment.
Job feels God has handed him over to wicked and ungodly people.

f.g: Job’s honest feeling — the reader knows from chapters 1–2 that Satan, not God’s hatred, is behind his trials.

n: Job was living in peace when God seemed to seize him by the neck, shake him apart, and set him up as a target.

f.w: set me up for his mark
f.g: Made me his target for arrows.

n: Surrounded by archers, Job feels pierced in his innermost being, his life spilled on the ground.

f.g: Kidneys — in Hebrew thought, the seat of the deepest emotions.
Bile; here a picture of his very life poured out.

n: Job is like a city wall battered breach after breach, with God charging at him like a mighty warrior.

f.g: Gap after gap broken in a wall during a siege.

n: Job has sewn rough mourning cloth onto his skin and laid his dignity in the dust.

f.g: Coarse goat-hair cloth worn in mourning and repentance.
A symbol of strength and honor; to put it in the dust is to be utterly humbled.

n: His face is red and swollen with weeping, and deep darkness hangs over his eyes.
Yet Job insists none of this is because of violence or wrongdoing on his part, and his prayers are sincere.
Like Abel’s blood crying from the ground, Job pleads with the earth not to cover his blood — let his cry for justice never be silenced.
Here is a breakthrough of faith: even now Job believes he has a witness in heaven who knows the truth and will vouch for him.

f.g: One who testifies — an advocate who will speak for him.

n: His friends mock him, but Job weeps his tears toward God — he keeps turning to the very One he cannot understand.

f.g: Can also be read “my interpreters (or spokesmen) are my friends” — the Hebrew is ambiguous.

n: Job longs for someone who could plead his case with God the way a person argues for a friend. Christians hear here a longing for Christ, the Advocate with the Father.

f.w: plead for a man with God

n: Job expects to die soon and take the road from which no one returns, so he wants his name cleared before then.

f.w: the way whence I shall not return
